sections.skill: Recognize a hallucination and why it happens

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination in AI output?

choices.text: A deliberate lie the tool chose to tell
An answer that is slow to arrive
False or unsupported output stated as true
A blurry image shown on a screen

questions.correct_answer: False or unsupported output stated as true
questions.intro: A HALLUCINATION is AI output that is false or unsupported but presented as if it were true: a made-up quote, a statistic with no source, a nonexistent book, a wrong date stated confidently. It happens because a language model generates likely-sounding text rather than looking facts up, so when it lacks the right information it can still produce something that fits the pattern of an answer. Hallucinations are more likely with obscure topics, very specific details (exact numbers, names, dates, page numbers) and questions about recent events. They are not lies in the human sense; they are errors.
questions.feedback: Confident but false or unsupported output.

sections.skill: Compare hallucination with a confident guesser at trivia night

questions.prompt: What does the teammate never say?

choices.text: "Good question"
"I don't know"
"Let's check"

questions.correct_answer: "I don't know"
questions.intro: At a trivia night, one teammate never says "I don't know." Asked the year a small town was founded, he says "1847" with total confidence. He is not lying on purpose; he just produces an answer that sounds right. Sometimes he is correct, sometimes not, and his tone is the same either way. A language model can act like this teammate. When it lacks the right information, it may still produce a confident, specific answer. That confident wrong answer is what people call a hallucination.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Why can careful reading alone not catch every hallucination?

choices.text: Hallucinations are always in red text
Hallucinations only appear in images
Invented details can look like real ones
Reading carefully makes errors appear

questions.correct_answer: Invented details can look like real ones
questions.intro: You cannot spot every hallucination by reading carefully, because invented details often look exactly like real ones. Some practical defenses: give the tool reliable source material to work from, ask it to say "I don't know" when the material does not contain an answer, and check specific details that matter in an independent source. Tools that search the web or cite documents reduce some hallucinations but can still misread or misquote sources. The habit that always helps is the same: verify the claims you will rely on.

questions.prompt: Which instruction helps reduce hallucinations when using supplied material?

choices.text: "If the text does not say, answer 'I don't know.'"
"Always give a complete answer, no matter what."
"Add extra details to be helpful."
"Sound as certain as possible."

questions.correct_answer: "If the text does not say, answer 'I don't know.'"
